title: Maitreya
hook: the coming Buddha, honored in Theravada and Mahayana alike

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samantabhadra on his white elephant, and vows as wide as space. Your line was great vows. Did your small one hold? Day one thousand one hundred eight.

A Pali sutta tells a long, dark story about the world going downhill. People grow more violent. Theft spreads, then killing, then lying, and human lives grow shorter and shorter. Then, at the bottom, something turns. People look at one another and decide to stop killing. Lives lengthen again. Slowly, the world grows good. And at that time, the Buddha says in the sutta, another Buddha will arise in the world, named Metteyya, teaching the same teaching he taught. Today, Maitreya, the Buddha still to come.
screen: `THE WORLD GOES DOWNHILL.` → `PEOPLE STOP KILLING.` → `ANOTHER BUDDHA WILL ARISE.`

segments.voice: First, a figure who is shared. Maitreya is the Sanskrit name; in Pali, Metteyya. He is named in the Pali texts that Theravada Buddhists keep, and he is honored across the Mahayana too. Schools differ on a great deal, and here is one hope they hold in common. Second, where he waits. Tradition says Maitreya now lives as a bodhisattva in the Tushita heaven, the same heaven where, the stories say, the bodhisattva who became Gotama Buddha waited before his last birth. He isn't a Buddha yet. He is preparing. Third, the faces. Some statues show Maitreya seated with both feet on the ground, as if about to stand up and come. And in China a wandering monk from the stories, round-bellied and laughing, with a cloth sack over his shoulder, came to be seen as one of Maitreya's forms. His name is Budai. If you have seen a laughing figure at a restaurant door or a temple gate, you may have met him. Fourth, what a coming Buddha says about now. Look again at the order in the Pali story. The new Buddha doesn't arrive and repair a broken world. People turn first. They give up killing, and decency returns one choice at a time, and only then does Metteyya arise. The future in that story is built out of ordinary kindness, long before anyone shining appears. Some Buddhists pray to meet Maitreya in a future life; others treat the hope as a reason to practice now. Either way, the hope doesn't ask anyone to sit and wait.
screen: `SHARED BY THERAVADA AND MAHAYANA.` · `WAITING IN TUSHITA.` · `FEET ON THE GROUND, READY.` · `PEOPLE TURN FIRST.` · then, large: `THE ONE TO COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Settle, and breathe. Picture a morning some years from now, in a place you know: your street, your kitchen, a school down the road. Picture it a little kinder than today. Not perfect. Just kinder: someone holding a door, a neighbor checking in, a tired person waved ahead in line. Let the picture get specific, with colors and voices. Then notice one thing in it that you could begin today. Rest with that, and let the picture fade back into the breath. The bell holds the time.
Maitreya. In Pali, Metteyya: the Buddha still to come, honored in Theravada and Mahayana alike. Today's word.
Your line: the one to come. Today, do one small, kind thing that belongs in the future you pictured. Tomorrow, Ksitigarbha. Day one thousand one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists in Theravada and Mahayana lands honor Maitreya as the Buddha to come; some dedicate merit in the hope of meeting him, and in China images of the laughing Budai stand at temple entrances.

fork.setup: the world has been sliding downhill for ages: more violence, shorter lives. in the Pali story, what turns it around?
options: people decide to stop killing, and decency returns
the new Buddha arrives and fixes everything
fork.reveal: people turn first. only after the world has grown good again does Metteyya arise.

original.note: Sanskrit; in Pali, Metteyya: the name of the Buddha who is still to come.

trapdoor: what you thought: the laughing, round-bellied Buddha.
what it means: Maitreya, the Buddha still to come, waiting as a bodhisattva; in China the laughing monk Budai came to be seen as one of his forms.
what a scholar hears: Metteyya in the Pali Cakkavatti-Sihanada Sutta, where the good age returns before he arises, a figure shared by Theravada and Mahayana.
recall: a factor that colors the knowing

notes: DN 26 paraphrased (Rhys Davids, Dialogues III, exists but is not quoted): decline in morality and lifespan, then people abstain from taking life and lifespan increases, and Metteyya arises. The sutta gives specific lifespans, left out under the claims rule. Confirm the order (theft, lying, killing) is fairly compressed.
Tushita as Maitreya's present abode and as where the bodhisattva Gotama waited before his last birth: stated as 'tradition says' and 'the stories say'.
'Some statues show Maitreya seated with both feet on the ground, as if about to stand': confirm as a fair description of the seated Maitreya iconography.
Budai as a form of Maitreya in Chinese tradition; the name-link between Maitreya and metta/maitri is left out under the claims rule (etymology).
Year three day 961 told Asanga and Maitreya; not repeated here.

Editor: hook order corrected to 'theft, then killing, then lying' (in DN 26 killing follows theft and weapons, and lying follows killing); 'the bodhisattva who became our Buddha' changed to 'Gotama Buddha' so the narrator does not speak as a believer.
